text: The crossing controller shall run a pedestrian crossing under a timing rule that is published as data, never show conflicting movements, and keep a ledger of who waited.
rationale: The product in one sentence. The rule is the thing a council decides; the ledger is how it sees what it decided.

text: The lamps shall never show a sequence that puts walkers and moving cars in the same space.
rationale: Safety comes before any argument about whose time matters.

text: Every lamp change shall follow the legal sequence CAR_GREEN, CAR_YELLOW, ALL_RED, WALK, PED_CLEAR, ALL_RED, CAR_GREEN, as judged by a conflict monitor that shares no code with the controller.
acceptance: C-SAFE-SEQ: 1000 seeded 24-hour runs under each published rule produce zero monitor faults.
rationale: Spike: 600 runs of 3 hours, 0 faults. Street hardware has an independent conflict monitor for the same reason.

text: Yellow shall last at least the configured yellow time, WALK at least the configured walk time, and pedestrian clearance at least crossing width divided by the design walking speed.
acceptance: C-SAFE-DWELL: across all C-SAFE-SEQ runs, the shortest observed dwell of each timed state is at least its configured minimum minus 1e-9 s.
rationale: The clearance interval is where a slow walker gets caught mid-road. Walking speed and width are placeholders until the authority's manual is read.

text: The conflict monitor shall detect every controller defect in a fixed set of seeded mutants.
acceptance: C-SAFE-BITE: each of at least 6 mutant controllers (all-red removed, yellow shortened, clearance shortened, WALK during yellow, green after WALK, double green) yields at least one monitor fault within 1 simulated hour.
rationale: A monitor that has never caught anything has not been shown to look. Spike: removing all-red gave 50 faults in 1 hour.

text: If the controller stops issuing lamp changes for longer than its longest legal dwell plus 2 seconds, the watchdog shall command the fail state.
acceptance: C-SAFE-FAILDARK: in 200 runs where the controller process is interrupted at a random time, the fail state is commanded within the bound every time, and in 1000 fault-free runs it is never commanded.
rationale: Software must not be the only safety layer; in the street the fail state is also enforced in hardware.

text: The controller shall do what the published rule says, and only that.
rationale: A rule that lives in code nobody reads is a rule nobody adopted.

text: The timing rule shall be a JSON document with a version, and the controller shall refuse to start on a rule that fails schema checks or that makes the pedestrian wait bound unreachable.
acceptance: C-RULE-DATA: 20 malformed or infeasible rules are each refused with the offending field named, including a 30 s wait bound with clearance plus all-red plus minimum green plus yellow plus all-red above 30 s; 3 valid rules start.
rationale: Spike rules were feasible by luck: 10 + 2 + 10 + 3 + 2 = 27 s against a 30 s bound.

text: Under a rule with a pedestrian wait bound, no pedestrian shall wait longer than the bound, measured from the button press.
acceptance: C-RULE-WAITCAP: over 1000 seeded 24-hour runs per bounded rule, the maximum wait from press to WALK is at most the bound; the maximum is recorded as a TPM.
rationale: Spike v1 measured from when the controller noticed the press and a 30 s promise became a 41.9 s wait. The promise runs on the walker's clock.

text: The controller shall receive every button press and every detector pulse it is sent, in order, with none dropped.
acceptance: C-RULE-NOLOSS: 10000 presses and pulses injected, including bursts of 50 at one instant, are all received in injection order and putsWaiting returns to 0.
rationale: des decision 11: a signal() loop drops simultaneous injections. The controller uses subscribe().

text: Under a rule marked pedestrian recall, WALK shall be served every cycle whether or not the button is pressed.
acceptance: C-RULE-RECALL: in 100 seeded runs with zero presses, the number of WALK intervals equals the number of cycles.
rationale: Whether walking requires asking is itself a rule a council can change.

text: The controller shall keep a ledger of delay by mode, so the cost of a rule shows up on the books of whoever pays it.
rationale: Signal timing has historically been judged on vehicle delay alone. A ledger with one column for walkers puts them on the books.

text: For each run, the ledger shall report person-seconds of delay for pedestrians and for car occupants, and their sum, from the same events that drove the lamps.
acceptance: C-LEDGER-SUM: on 50 hand-built scripted arrival sequences, ledger totals equal hand-computed totals to within 1e-9 s per person.
rationale: The ledger is only as good as its arithmetic; scripted cases make it checkable by hand.

text: Given two published rules, the tool shall simulate both on common random numbers and report the change in each mode's delay with a 95 percent interval.
acceptance: C-LEDGER-COMPARE: on a synthetic crossing whose true difference is known from 1e6 simulated hours, the reported 95 percent interval covers it in 93 to 97 percent of 2000 repetitions (about plus or minus 4.1 binomial SE; a correct interval fails this under 1 in 10000 runs, one with 90 percent true coverage essentially never passes). Each repetition is 20 paired seeds of 24 h per rule. The truth is computed once and stored with its seed list and its own SE. The check runs on a schedule (about 50 CPU-minutes), not on every commit.
rationale: Spike (synthetic street, not validated): gap-seeking and car-first both total about 37.5 person-hours a day, but walkers carry 4.8 of it instead of 11.9. Claims like that need an error bar before a council reads them. Council round 1: band was first set on 400 repetitions, only about 1.8 SE, so a correct interval would have failed about 7 percent of the time; Modulo caught it. Council round 2: repetition length was unstated, which left both a cost and a loophole (short repetitions push a normal interval into undercoverage); Modulo measured it and fixed the shape.

text: While XW-FIELD is not verified, the comparison tool shall print the label synthetic street, not validated on every figure it reports.
acceptance: C-LEDGER-LABEL: on 20 rule pairs with XW-FIELD unverified, every table row and every JSON record the tool writes carries the label; on the same pairs with a fixture marking XW-FIELD verified, none does.
rationale: Council round 2: XW-FIELD forbade showing a council any comparison before field validation, and this council broke that rule in round 1. The label belongs in the tool that prints the numbers, not in the habits of whoever writes the report, because a habit is what gets dropped first.

text: The same model code shall run under run() and under runRealtime() with a fake clock and give identical traces.
acceptance: C-TWIN: 7 simulated days per published rule, trace arrays compared entry by entry (time, priority, kind, label), zero differences.
rationale: This is what lets offline verification say anything about the live controller. Spike: 103689 entries over 24 h, zero differences.

text: The simulated street shall reproduce counts and waits observed at a real crossing.
acceptance: C-FIELD: on one week of logged presses, detector pulses and lamp changes from a real crossing, simulated mean pedestrian wait and mean car delay per hour lie within 15 percent of the logged values in at least 90 percent of hours.
rationale: Stays unverified in this lab, and vv must keep showing it that way. The 15 percent bound is a placeholder. Round 2: the clause about councils moved to XW-LEDGER-LABEL, where a test can hold it.
